ideas.title: Vault Breakers
ideas.concept: A heist crew races through a bank's floor plan gathering partial clues about a hidden 3-symbol vault code, then tests guesses on a real rotating combination dial mounted in the Vault Chamber. Every turn the shared Alarm die ticks a security track upward, so the longer anyone dithers, the less the eventual haul is worth. A turn feels like: move your operative, peek a clue chip from the room you land in, mentally update your suspect grid, and decide whether you know enough to risk a public dial test.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: Clue/Cluedo's movement + room-based clue-gathering + solo accusation skeleton. Genuine rule changes: (1) the guess-input is a physical 3-ring rotating dial players manipulate in real time instead of naming a card triple; (2) clues come from per-room chip bags drawn blind by the visiting player (no hand-holding/disproving of other players' cards, so it plays with 3-5 without needing 3+ 'other hands' to function); (3) a shared Alarm track adds a real-time value-decay pressure absent from Clue, where the total loot pool shrinks each time the Alarm advances. Searched 'board game rotating combination dial lock deduction game physical cryptex', 'deduction board game with rotating disc dial reveal solution mechanism', and 'Cryptex boardgamegeek 426522 heist deduction gameplay mechanism' — found 3D-printed cryptex hardware and an unrelated BGG title called Cryptex (a 'crypto adventure', not a movement/deduction game), but no shipped board game combining room-movement clue-gathering with a player-facing rotating multi-ring test dial and a shared escalating alarm-value-decay track.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players, ages 10+, 45-60 min. SETUP: Assemble the Vault Chamber piece (3 stacked rotating rings, each showing 6 engraved symbols, behind a hinged privacy cover). Without looking, one player draws 3 symbol chips blind from the shared chip bag (one per ring) and slots them face-down into the covered Solution Tray, then closes and pins the tray shut — no one, including that player, sees the result. Place the 6 Room tiles (Security Office, Records Room, Camera Bay, Staff Lounge, Loading Dock, Vault Chamber) in a ring connected by printed corridor paths. Each non-Vault room gets its own small clue bag containing symbol-elimination chips (e.g. 'Ring 2 is NOT the gear'). Each player takes a crew meeple on the Loading Dock start space and a personal 3-slot Notes rack. Set the Alarm peg to 0 on the shared Alarm track (max 8) and the Loot dial to 100%. TURN (clockwise): (1) Move your meeple 1-3 spaces along corridors (your choice). (2) If you entered a non-Vault room this turn, draw 1 chip blind from that room's bag, read it privately, and either keep it on your Notes rack or discard it face down (bluff option — you may 'discard' a chip you actually keep by placing a spare blank chip instead, once per game). (3) Roll the Alarm die: on a lock icon, advance the Alarm peg 1 space; every time it crosses a marked threshold, the Loot dial drops one tier (100%->75%->50%->25%). (4) If you are in the Vault Chamber, you may set the 3 rings to your guessed combination and make one Accusation this game: open the Solution Tray's sliding window to compare. Correct = you win immediately, take the full current Loot % as your score. Incorrect = permanently flip your meeple face-down (out of future accusations, but you keep drawing clues and can still win on tiebreak scoring). GAME END: if all players have accused incorrectly, or the Alarm reaches max (vault auto-locks), the game ends with no winner via accusation — instead, whoever holds the most correct never-discarded clue chips (verified by finally opening the tray) wins on knowledge. SCORING/WIN: first correct accusation wins outright at current Loot %; otherwise the best-informed player wins.
ideas.components: 1x Vault Chamber assembly (PLA, ~10cm dia base, 3 stacked rotating symbol rings on a central peg + hinged privacy cover with sliding window, snap-fit peg tolerance 0.3mm clearance); 6x Room tiles (PLA, 8x8cm flat tiles, engraved room art + corridor connector notches); 1x Solution Tray with pinned lid (PLA, 6x4cm, holds 3 chips, removable print-in-place pin); ~30x symbol chips across 6 small drawstring-substitute printed chip-cups (PLA, 2cm hex chips, 6 engraved symbols, plus blank 'bluff' chips); 5x crew meeples (PLA, 3cm painted pawns, 5 colors); 5x personal Notes racks (PLA, 10x3cm slotted tray, 3 slots each); 1x Alarm track board insert (PLA, 15cm linear track, 0-8) with 1 alarm peg; 1x Loot % dial (PLA, 6cm rotating pointer disc, 4 tiers); 1x custom d6 Alarm die (PLA, 1.6cm, 2 lock-icon faces, 4 blank faces); box (corrugate-substitute rigid printed-lid box, 20x20x6cm).
ideas.demand_case: Deduction is one of BoardGameGeek's largest listed mechanic categories (thousands of tagged titles), and social-deduction/whodunit games are a proven mainstream-family category anchored by the decades-long popularity of Cluedo/Clue as a household name — evidence that a movement + clue-gathering + accusation structure has durable broad appeal beyond hobbyists. Target audience: family game night and casual group players, ages 10+, who already know 'guess the secret' games but want a heavier physical/tactile hook than a card envelope.
ideas.fun_case: The core tension each turn is a public-information budgeting problem: reveal more of the map for clues (safe, but the Alarm punishes everyone's payout) versus commit early to an accusation on partial information (risky, one-shot per player). That push-pull between patience and payout decay is the same lever that makes Clue's 'do I have enough to accuse' moment satisfying, but the visible physical dial and shared shrinking pot make the tension legible to the whole table at once rather than hidden in one player's head, which comparable party-deduction hybrids like Deception: Murder in Hong Kong and classic Clue show sustains replayability at family-night length (45-60 min).
ideas.producibility_notes: 9 distinct part types, ~55 total pieces, no paper cards (all clue text is symbol-only, engraved). Riskiest feature is the Vault Chamber's 3 stacked rotating rings on a single peg: this is a known, widely-proven FDM joint type (equivalent to a 3D-printed cryptex, confirmed printable at consumer scale by existing hobbyist cryptex designs), so it does not need physical iteration to validate the underlying mechanism — only a stated clearance tolerance (0.3mm per ring) needs to be held during slicing. The sliding-window lid on the Solution Tray is a simple channel-and-tab slide, also a standard low-risk joint. No feature is under 1mm; smallest engraved symbol recess is 2mm wide, safe for 0.4mm nozzle FDM. No metal hardware/inserts required.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a heist-themed board game on a dark wood table: an open square box lid printed with bold vault-door art in copper and charcoal titled 'VAULT BREAKERS'. In front, a ring of six hexagonal room tiles arranged around a central cylindrical vault prop with three stacked rotating rings showing engraved symbols (gear, flame, key, eye, arrow, skull) visible through a brass-colored window, plus a small hinged lid. Around it: five painted pawn meeples in red, blue, green, yellow, purple; small hex chips with engraved symbols; a curved alarm track piece with a red peg; a rotating percentage dial. Warm dramatic spotlighting, copper/charcoal/black color palette, slightly cinematic heist-movie mood, all pieces crisply 3D-printed matte plastic.

ideas.title: Tidal Kingdoms
ideas.concept: Players draft hex tiles to grow rival island kingdoms, but every two rounds the sea physically rises: a new tide ring stacks onto the central post and any low-lying tile is flipped to its drowned side, wiping out its score. A turn feels like: pick the best available terrain tile knowing it might drown in a few rounds, and decide whether to build wide now or stack elevation to survive the next flood.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'area control board game rising sea level physical stacking rings submerge tiles' and 'land above sea below rising tide tile board game mechanic' — found only a same-named digital/Steam puzzle game (Land Above Sea Below, not a physical board game) and Pandemic: Rising Tide (a dike-building card-driven Euro with no physical elevation/submersion component). No shipped board game was found where a stacking physical ring track on the board itself permanently flips low tiles to a scoreless 'submerged' face as the game progresses; existing rising-water games represent flooding abstractly via cards or tracks rather than a tactile elevation mechanism that physically covers tile ranks.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 45 min. SETUP: Place the circular Archipelago frame in the table center with the Tide Post (a peg tower) at its middle. Shuffle the 48 double-sided hex terrain tiles (one side = terrain type + elevation number 1, 2, or 3 printed on the corner; flip side = plain 'submerged' blue) into the draw bag. Reveal 4 tiles face-up terrain-side in the Market row. Each player takes a Kingdom mat, 10 population cubes, and places one starting tile adjacent to the frame edge nearest them. TURN ORDER: snake draft. On your turn: (1) take one tile from the Market row (its position in the row, left to right, determines minor bonus resources — leftmost tiles give 1 bonus population cube); (2) place it edge-adjacent to any of your own placed tiles, terrain-side up, elevation number visible; (3) refill the Market row from the bag. TIDE EVENT: after every 2nd full round (tracked on the Round marker), before the next draft, add one Tide Ring onto the Tide Post (5 rings total across the game) and immediately flip every placed tile on the whole shared board whose elevation number is <= the number of rings currently on the post to its blue submerged side (submerged tiles score 0 and block future adjacency scoring but tiles may still be placed adjacent to them). SCORING: game ends after the 5th Tide Ring is placed. Each player scores: 1 point per unsubmerged tile in their largest single connected same-terrain-type cluster (mountains beat forests beat fields beat coast, ties broken by cluster size), plus 1 point per population cube spent to 'reinforce' a tile pre-emptively (an action that costs 2 population cubes to permanently protect one of your tiles from ever submerging, taken instead of drafting on your turn). Highest total wins; ties broken by most unsubmerged tiles owned.
ideas.components: 1x Archipelago frame board (PLA, 30cm diameter ring with hex sockets, flat, 4mm thick); 1x Tide Post peg (PLA, 8cm tall center peg fixed to frame); 5x stackable Tide Rings (PLA, 3cm inner dia washers, 1cm tall, snap-stack onto post); 48x double-sided hex terrain tiles (PLA two-color swap or single-color engraved both faces, 4cm flat-to-flat, elevation numbers 1-3 engraved); 4x Kingdom player mats (PLA, 15x10cm flat reference boards); 40x population cubes (PLA, 1cm cubes, 4 colors x10); 1x Round marker track (PLA, 10cm linear track with peg); box (printed-lid rigid box, 30x30x7cm).
ideas.demand_case: Tile-laying/area-control is one of BGG's top mechanic categories by title count, and family-weight tile-drafting games (Kingdomino, Cascadia, Karuba) are consistently among the best-selling modern board games at mainstream retail, evidencing a large audience for 'draft-a-tile, grow-your-area' gameplay. Target audience: family and gateway-hobbyist gamers, ages 10+, who enjoy Kingdomino/Cascadia-style tile drafting and want a stronger table-presence physical gimmick.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a timing bet: commit population resources to permanently save a low tile now (costly, certain) versus gamble that you'll reach the next elevation tier before the tide catches up (free, risky) — the same 'build now vs. build safe' tension that makes Kingdomino and Cascadia's spatial puzzle engaging, but made physically visible and irreversible via the stacking ring, so players can see exactly how much time is left before committing, which comparable elevation/timing-pressure games in the tile-laying category show sustains tension without adding rules-reading overhead for a 45-minute family slot.
ideas.producibility_notes: 7 distinct part types, ~100 total pieces (dominated by cheap small cubes and tiles). No paper cards; all tile info is engraved geometry (elevation pips as raised dots doubled with printed numerals for accessibility). Riskiest joint is the Tide Ring stack-and-peg: 5 identical rings on one post is a repeated known-behavior friction/snap-stack joint (not a novel mechanism), and because all 5 rings are geometrically identical, only one tolerance needs validating, then it repeats safely — this is a low, well-understood risk, not a compounding one. No feature under 1mm (smallest engraved elevation numeral is 3mm). No hardware inserts needed; post-and-ring is single-material PLA-on-PLA with a stated 0.4mm radial clearance.
ideas.prompt: Overhead product photo of a nautical-themed board game: a circular archipelago board made of matte teal and sandy-tan hexagonal tiles depicting mountains, forests, fields, and coastline, arranged in a ring on a round frame. In the center rises a short wooden-look peg post with three stacked translucent blue plastic rings around it like tide markers, and two of the outer hex tiles are flipped to show a plain wave-pattern blue 'submerged' underside. Small colored population cubes (red, blue, green, yellow) sit on player mats at the table edges. Square box beside it with lid art showing a rising wave over an island silhouette, titled 'TIDAL KINGDOMS' in bold nautical lettering. Bright natural lighting, teal/sand/coral color palette, crisp clean 3D-printed plastic finish.

ideas.title: Freight Line
ideas.concept: Players jointly build one shared rail network on a communal hex board, but every round each player's own locomotive automatically races out from its home depot along whatever track exists, scoring only the fresh track it actually crosses. A turn feels like: place a track tile to extend the network toward where you want to go next round, then watch your engine (and your rivals') roll out and grab the hexes it reaches first.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: hex edge-matching connection games (Tantrix/Serpentiles-style path tiles) crossed with round-based tile-drafting network games like Railroad Tiles. Genuine rule change: instead of each player building on a private tableau (Railroad Tiles) or simply completing loops for static scoring (Tantrix), all players build into ONE shared board and every round every player's Engine token physically moves along the completed network from a fixed home Depot, scoring only newly-crossed hexes that round — turning tile placement into a positional prediction of where your own engine will be forced to travel next, not just a static pattern match. Searched 'tile laying pipe network connection board game hex tiles double sided routes twist' and 'tile laying game engine locomotive token moves along completed track scores route each round' — found Serpentiles/Tantrix-family static path-matching games and Railroad Tiles (individual player boards, token-queue scoring, no shared-board engine-movement race); no shipped game combines a single shared communal network with automatic per-round engine movement scoring.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 40 min. SETUP: Assemble the hex board frame (empty sockets). Each player places a Depot marker tile on a distinct edge hex of the frame and puts their Engine token on it. Shuffle 60 double-ended track tiles (each shows 2-3 route paths connecting different edges of the hexagon) into a bag; reveal 4 face-up in the Market row. TURN (in player order): (1) take one tile from the Market row, place it into any empty socket on the shared board so that at least one of its route paths connects to an already-placed tile's path (first tile of the game may be placed anywhere adjacent to a Depot); refill the Market row. (2) After all players have placed one tile this round (i.e., once per full round, not every individual turn), resolve Engine Movement simultaneously: each Engine advances hex-by-hex along any continuous connected path starting from its Depot, always taking the path not yet fully explored by that engine if a fork exists (player's choice at forks), stopping when it reaches a dead end, an already-fully-scored hex, or has moved a number of hexes equal to the current Round number (engines get faster each round). Each hex an Engine enters for the first time this game scores that player 1 point (2 points if it is a Terminus hex, of which there are 6 fixed around the board's outer rim). GAME END: when the tile bag is empty and one full round of movement has resolved, or when all 6 Terminus hexes have been reached by someone. SCORING: sum all hex points earned across the game; player with the most points wins; ties broken by whoever reached the most Terminus hexes.
ideas.components: 1x hex board frame (PLA, 35cm across, sockets for ~60 hexes plus 6 marked Terminus hexes); 60x double-ended track tiles (PLA, 5cm flat-to-flat hexagons, engraved route-path grooves, single color per player-neutral set); 4x Depot markers (PLA, 3cm flat tokens, 4 colors); 4x Engine tokens (PLA, 2.5cm painted locomotive-silhouette pawns, 4 colors); 1x Round tracker (PLA, 8cm linear track with peg, marks current round/engine speed); box (printed-lid rigid box, 25x25x6cm).
ideas.demand_case: Tile-laying and route/network-building are both long-established top-tier BGG mechanic categories, and train/network games (Ticket to Ride family, Railroad Tiles, the 18xx family) represent one of the best-documented sustained hobbyist and family niches in board gaming, evidencing durable demand for 'connect the network' gameplay at multiple weights. Target audience: gateway-to-mid-weight hobbyists and family groups, ages 10+, who enjoy Ticket to Ride-style route building but want a shared-board puzzle rather than a hand-management card game.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is spatial forecasting under shared contention: place a tile to extend the network toward hexes YOU want your engine to reach next round, knowing opponents' engines may reach the same fresh track first and steal the point before you do — a race-the-clock variant of the placement tension that makes Kingdomino/Tsuro-style tile games engaging, sharpened by the fact that the payoff (engine movement) is delayed and partially shared, which comparable connection games (Tsuro's forced-movement-along-a-shared-board tension in particular) show keeps a light ruleset replayable across many short games.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 distinct part types, ~70 total pieces, all game info conveyed via engraved route grooves (no cards, no printed text needed to play). Track tiles are flat engraved hexagons with no moving parts — very low risk, same class as existing Tantrix/Serpentiles-style printed tile sets already sold on hobbyist marketplaces, so the geometry is proven producible. Depot and Engine tokens are simple flat/pawn shapes. No feature under 1mm (route groove width 4mm, safe for 0.4mm nozzle). No hardware, hinges, or friction-fit assemblies required anywhere in this game — lowest-risk producibility profile of this batch.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a railway-themed board game on a warm oak table: a large hexagonal frame board filled with matte hexagon tiles engraved with curving railway track grooves in brass-gold, forming a sprawling connected network, with a few bright red 'Terminus' hexes glowing at the rim. Four small painted locomotive-shaped pawn tokens in red, blue, green, and yellow sit at depot markers on the board's edges. A stack of extra unplaced hex tiles sits beside the board. A rectangular box with lid art of crossing rail lines radiating from a central hub, titled 'FREIGHT LINE' in bold industrial lettering. Warm directional lighting, brass/oak/cream color palette, crisp matte 3D-printed plastic tiles.

ideas.title: Orchard Order
ideas.concept: Players draft fruit chips one at a time from a rotating carousel tray that physically spins a notch after every pick, building a personal orchard grid for pattern bonuses. A turn feels like: grab the best chip in front of you, watch the carousel turn toward the next player, and start reading two turns ahead to guess what will rotate into your reach.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: card-drafting pattern-building games (Sushi Go's hand-passing draft, Sagrada/Azul's shared-pool drafting for a personal grid). Genuine rule change: the shared pool is a single physical rotating carousel disc with fixed pockets that spins one position after every individual pick (not after a full round, and not via passing hands around the table), so the pool itself moves predictably and continuously rather than jumping in a hand-sized batch — creating a positional-timing read ('what rotates into reach in 2 picks') that hand-passing and static-pool-refill drafting don't have. Searched 'lazy susan rotating tray card drafting board game mechanism spin' and 'rotating carousel drafting pool board game mechanic pockets' — found only furniture/DIY lazy-susan uses for convenience (rotating a static board to face a player) and patent filings for generic rotating game boards, no shipped drafting game where the pool itself is a continuously-rotating fixed-pocket carousel that turns after every single pick.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 8+, 30 min. SETUP: Place the Carousel (a 6-pocket rotating disc) in the center, fill all 6 pockets with fruit chips drawn blind from the chip bag. Each player takes a 5x5 Orchard Grid mat and sits around the carousel so one pocket aligns in front of each seat (with 2-3 players, some pockets sit between seats and are 'open' picks anyone may take on their turn). TURN (clockwise): (1) take the one chip currently aligned directly in front of you (or, if none is aligned to your seat, any one open unaligned pocket) and place it into any empty cell of your Orchard Grid, following the placement rule: a chip must be placed orthogonally adjacent to at least one already-placed chip on your grid (first chip of the game may go anywhere); (2) refill the pocket you just emptied with a new chip drawn blind from the bag; (3) rotate the Carousel one pocket position clockwise, so a new chip is now aligned to you for next time it's your turn. SCORING (end of game, when any player fills their grid or the chip bag is empty): score each completed row of your grid that is all the same fruit type (3 points), each completed column with 5 different fruit types (5 points), and 1 point per chip placed adjacent to a matching-type chip anywhere on your grid. Highest total wins; ties broken by most complete rows.
ideas.components: 1x Carousel disc (PLA, 18cm diameter, 6 pocket wells 3cm each, mounted on a low-friction center pivot post/washer joint); ~60x fruit chips (PLA, 2.5cm hex chips, engraved with 6 fruit icons: apple, pear, grape, plum, fig, citrus, single color per fruit type via multi-color print or paint-fill); 4x Orchard Grid mats (PLA, 15x15cm flat 5x5 grid boards); box (printed-lid rigid box, 22x22x6cm).
ideas.demand_case: Drafting is one of BGG's most represented mechanic tags, and pattern-building drafters in this exact weight class (Sagrada, Azul, Sushi Go) are consistently among the top-selling modern family games at retail, evidencing strong existing demand for 'draft a piece, build a grid' gameplay at a 30-minute family weight. Target audience: family game night and light-hobbyist players, ages 8+, who already enjoy Azul/Sushi Go-style drafting.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a two-layer read: which chip do I take now for my own grid, and which chip am I leaving behind that will rotate toward an opponent versus rotate away from the table entirely — the same 'take the best thing before it's gone or gets worse for me' tension that makes Sushi Go and Azul engaging, but the continuous single-step rotation (rather than hand-passing in a batch) makes the future pool state something players can track and plan for turn-by-turn, adding a light forecasting skill on top of the familiar drafting core that comparable pattern-drafters show holds attention for repeat 30-minute plays.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 distinct part types, ~65 total pieces, no cards (all fruit types are engraved/color-coded chips). Riskiest feature is the Carousel's center pivot: a flat disc rotating on a peg-and-washer joint is a well-proven, low-tolerance-sensitivity FDM mechanism (equivalent to many existing printable spinner/lazy-susan game accessories), not a novel or unvalidated joint — a stated 0.4mm clearance between disc bore and post is sufficient and does not require physical prototyping to reason about. No feature under 1mm (smallest fruit icon engraving is 4mm). No metal hardware required if the post is printed integral to the base; a thin layer of printed smooth washer prevents wobble.
ideas.prompt: Bright product photo of a cheerful family board game: a circular wooden-look rotating carousel tray in the center of the table with six shallow pockets holding colorful engraved fruit-shaped chips (red apple, green pear, purple grape, orange fig, yellow citrus, plum), sitting on a low center pivot. Around it, four square flat grid mats printed with a 5x5 lattice, some cells filled with fruit chips. A square box with lid art showing a stylized spinning orchard wheel bursting with fruit, titled 'ORCHARD ORDER' in playful rounded lettering. Cheerful bright lighting, orchard palette of reds, greens, purples and yellows against natural wood tones, crisp matte 3D-printed plastic chips.

ideas.title: Ironforge Hollow
ideas.concept: A dwarven-forge-themed retelling of classic Mancala (Kalah rules): players sow cast ore nuggets around a ring of crucible pits, racing to bank the most metal in their furnace before the mine runs dry. A turn feels like: pick a crucible, sow its ore one pit at a time around the ring, and hope your last nugget lands in your own furnace for a free extra turn.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Mancala (standard Kalah ruleset, public-domain traditional game, no rule change). Styling concept: dwarven blacksmith forge theme — the two rows of 6 pits become hexagonal 'crucible' molds carved into a stone-textured board, the 48 seeds become two-tone cast 'ore nugget' tokens (copper and iron-colored), and the two end stores become forge firebox-shaped 'Furnace' collection bins with flame-relief detailing. Searched 'mancala reskinned themed board game bees pollen harvest' (found Beehive Mancala, an existing published bee-themed reskin — confirming the general reskin category is viable but that exact bee theme is taken) and 'mancala reskin dwarven forge ore gems themed board game' (found only generic gem-filled mancala sets and an unrelated worker-placement game called Dwarven Miner; no existing product combines Mancala's ruleset with a dwarven-forge/crucible/furnace styling concept).
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 6+, 15-20 min. Standard Kalah Mancala rules, reskinned. SETUP: the board has two rows of 6 Crucible pits (6 per player, facing them) plus one Furnace store at each end (to each player's right). Place 4 ore nuggets in each of the 12 Crucibles; Furnaces start empty. TURN: choose one of your own non-empty Crucibles, pick up all its nuggets, and sow them one at a time counter-clockwise into each following pit (Crucibles and your own Furnace only — skip the opponent's Furnace entirely), including opponent's Crucibles if you have enough nuggets to reach that far. SPECIAL RULES: if your last sown nugget lands in your own empty Furnace, take another turn immediately. If your last sown nugget lands in one of your own empty Crucibles (and that landing pit was empty before this sowing), capture that nugget plus all nuggets in the directly opposite opponent Crucible, moving them all to your Furnace. GAME END: when a player's entire row of 6 Crucibles is empty at the start of their turn, the game ends; the other player sweeps all remaining nuggets on their side into their own Furnace. SCORING/WIN: whoever has the most nuggets in their Furnace wins.
ideas.components: 1x forge board (PLA, 40x18cm, 12 hexagonal crucible-mold pits + 2 firebox-shaped furnace bins with flame relief detail, stone-texture surface finish); 48x ore nuggets (PLA, 1.5cm rounded nugget tokens, 24 copper-tone + 24 iron-tone via dual-color print or paint-fill); box (printed-lid rigid box, 42x20x5cm, doubles as nugget storage tray under a removable board panel).
ideas.demand_case: Mancala is one of the oldest and most widely played traditional abstract games in the world, with dedicated Mancala board sales sustained across mass retail (Amazon/Walmart) and a documented published reskin precedent (Beehive Mancala, sold through museum gift shops and general retail) proving that themed Mancala sets have real standalone retail demand beyond the plain wooden version. Target audience: families and casual/traditional-game buyers, ages 6+, looking for a well-known, easy-to-teach 2-player game with distinctive tabletop presence.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a well-proven one: which pit to sow from to either land your last piece in your own store (free turn) or set up a capture of the opponent's pit, a tight short-loop calculation that has kept Mancala variants popular across cultures for centuries. The forge theme adds no new decision but strengthens table presence and gift appeal, which comparable themed abstract reskins (Beehive Mancala's continued retail availability) validate as a real driver of purchase for an already-proven ruleset.
ideas.producibility_notes: 2 distinct part types, 49 total pieces (dominated by identical small nugget tokens). No cards, no rulebook-dependent components — this is a pure geometry-and-token game. Lowest-complexity producibility profile in this batch: no joints, hinges, or moving assemblies at all; the only design consideration is pit depth (must comfortably hold up to ~24 nuggets during play without spilling, so a minimum 2.5cm pit depth is specified). No feature under 1mm. Fully single-print-run friendly.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a fantasy dwarven-forge-themed board game: a long dark stone-textured rectangular board carved with two rows of six hexagonal crucible-mold pits filled with small round two-tone ore nugget tokens (bright copper-orange and dark iron-grey), flanked at each end by a raised firebox-shaped furnace bin with engraved flame relief details in a warm bronze color. Rustic rectangular box beside it with lid art of a glowing forge and anvil, titled 'IRONFORGE HOLLOW' in bold hammered-metal lettering. Warm forge-fire lighting, palette of charcoal grey, bronze, and molten orange, crisp matte 3D-printed stone-finish plastic.

ideas.title: Coral Court
ideas.concept: A coral-reef-themed retelling of classic Nine Men's Morris: two players place and later slide coral-polyp tokens around three nested reef rings, trying to align three in a row to snap off an opponent's polyp. A turn feels like: place or slide a polyp to threaten a row while blocking your opponent's forming line, tension ratcheting up as the board fills.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Nine Men's Morris (standard 'mill' ruleset — placement phase, movement phase, flying phase at 3 pieces remaining — public-domain traditional game, no rule change). Styling concept: coral reef ecosystem — the three concentric square rings become three concentric organic reef-ring channels connected by radial coral branches, the 18 pieces become pink and purple coral-polyp-shaped tokens, and a captured piece is described as 'bleaching' rather than being removed. Searched 'nine men's morris reskin sci-fi themed board game space outpost' (found an existing published sci-fi reskin, Spaceship Morris on TheGameCrafter — confirming the reskin category works but that theme is taken) and 'nine men's morris reskin coral reef ocean themed board game' (no results found for any coral/reef/ocean-themed reskin of Nine Men's Morris; the theme is unclaimed).
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 8+, 20-30 min. Standard Nine Men's Morris (mill) rules, reskinned. SETUP: the board shows 3 concentric reef rings connected by 4 radial coral branches, forming 24 intersection points. Each player has 9 coral-polyp tokens (pink or purple) held off-board at the start. PHASE 1 (Placement): players alternate placing one polyp on any empty intersection point. Whenever a player completes a straight line of exactly 3 of their own polyps along a ring or branch (a 'reef cluster'), they immediately remove one opponent polyp of their choice from the board (may not remove a polyp that is currently part of the opponent's own completed cluster unless no other polyp is removable). After all 18 polyps are placed, proceed to Phase 2. PHASE 2 (Movement): players alternate sliding one of their own polyps to an empty adjacent connected point (along a drawn line only); forming a reef cluster this way also removes an opponent polyp under the same rule. PHASE 3 (Flying): once a player is reduced to exactly 3 polyps remaining, that player may on their turns move a polyp to ANY empty point on the board (not just adjacent), while their opponent (if still above 3) continues normal adjacent movement. GAME END/WIN: a player wins immediately when their opponent is reduced to 2 polyps (cannot form a cluster) or has no legal move available on their turn.
ideas.components: 1x reef board (PLA, 30x30cm flat board, 3 concentric ring channels + 4 radial branch grooves engraved with coral-texture relief, 24 marked intersection points); 18x coral-polyp tokens (PLA, 2cm branching-coral-shaped pegs that seat into board divots, 9 pink + 9 purple); box (printed-lid rigid box, 32x32x5cm).
ideas.demand_case: Nine Men's Morris is one of the most historically widespread traditional abstract strategy games (documented board carvings dating back millennia across multiple continents), and it remains in active mass-market retail today as wooden and travel sets (Amazon/WE Games/Etsy listings), with at least one other published themed reskin (Spaceship Morris) validating that a themed physical version of this exact ruleset has a real audience. Target audience: families and abstract-strategy traditional-game buyers, ages 8+, seeking a well-known 2-player game with a fresh decorative theme for gifting or display.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is the well-established Nine Men's Morris tension between building your own threatened line and blocking the opponent's, sharpened further once pieces start moving and both players must weigh mobility against defensive positioning — a tight, quick-to-learn abstract puzzle that has sustained this exact ruleset's popularity for centuries and continues to justify new retail editions today (per the Spaceship Morris precedent), which the coral theme leverages purely for shelf appeal without changing the proven decision space.
ideas.producibility_notes: 2 distinct part types, 19 total pieces. No cards. The only joint consideration is the polyp tokens seating into shallow board divots (a simple peg-in-shallow-recess friction fit, not a locking joint, so pieces must lift out freely during the sliding/flying phases) — a well-understood, low-risk feature already common in printed abstract-game sets. No feature under 1mm (engraved ring/branch grooves are 5mm wide). No hardware or hinges anywhere in this design.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of an ocean-reef-themed abstract strategy board game: a flat square board in coral-white and turquoise, engraved with three concentric organic ring channels connected by four radial branch grooves textured like coral, dotted with 24 shallow intersection divots. Small branching coral-shaped peg tokens sit at intersections, half in vivid pink and half in deep purple. A square box beside it with lid art of a vibrant coral reef scene, titled 'CORAL COURT' in flowing aquatic lettering. Bright underwater-inspired lighting, turquoise/coral-pink/purple color palette, crisp glossy-finish 3D-printed plastic pieces.

ideas.title: Rune Trick
ideas.concept: A trick-taking game played with double-ended rune tiles where you choose which symbol faces up when you play, and the winner of each trick spins a central dial to set the next trump. A turn feels like: read the trick so far, decide which half of your tile to commit to the table, and weigh whether to burn your best rune now or save it for when you control the dial.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: domino-based trick-taking (Texas 42-style, where a tile's suit is fixed automatically by its higher-numbered end). Genuine rule change: (1) each tile shows two different rune SUIT symbols (not numeric pips) and the player playing it actively chooses which half faces up as the led/followed suit for that trick, a live strategic decision rather than a fixed pip-value rule; (2) trump is not fixed for the whole hand but re-set every single trick by the previous trick's winner rotating a central Trump Dial to any symbol shown among the tiles just played, creating a dynamic shifting-trump metagame absent from standard domino trick-taking. Searched 'trick-taking game double-ended domino tiles orientation changes trump rule' and 'domino trick taking game player chooses orientation suit each play dynamic trump' — found Texas 42 and Double Takes, both of which fix suit/trump by the domino's pip values or hold doubles as a static permanent trump; no domino/tile trick-taking game was found where the active player freely chooses tile orientation each play and trump is dynamically re-set every trick by the winner.
ideas.rules: 4 players in 2 fixed partnerships (seated alternating), ages 12+, 40-60 min. SETUP: shuffle the 42 double-ended rune tiles (7 rune symbols, each tile showing 2 of the 7 symbols on its two halves, all 21 unique symbol-pairs plus doubles printed twice for a 42-tile set) face down and deal 10-11 tiles to each player (uneven deal on last player, set aside remainder as a blind kitty worth bonus points to the first trick's winner). Place the Trump Dial (6 rune symbols around a rotating pointer, no symbol pre-selected) in the center. HAND: the dealer's left-hand player leads first. LEADING: the leader plays one tile from hand, choosing which of its two halves faces up — that symbol is the led suit for the trick. FOLLOWING: each other player in turn must play a tile that has the led suit symbol on EITHER half, orienting it so the matching symbol faces up (if they have no tile showing the led suit on either half, they may play any tile oriented however they choose — an automatic 'off-suit' discard). WINNING A TRICK: highest-value tile showing the current Trump Dial symbol (if any was played) wins the trick regardless of led suit; if no trump was played, the highest-value tile of the led suit wins (tile values are printed 0-6 per half, independent of which half is up). The trick winner collects the trick, adds its point-value tiles (tiles marked with a star are worth 5 or 10 points, all others 0) to their partnership's score pile, then rotates the Trump Dial pointer to any ONE symbol that appeared face-up anywhere in the trick just won, setting trump for the next trick only. SCORING/WIN: play all tricks in the hand; total each partnership's collected star-tile points plus 1 point per trick won. First partnership to 150 points across multiple hands wins.
ideas.components: 42x double-ended rune tiles (PLA, 5x2.5cm rectangular dominoes, engraved rune symbols on each half plus small value numerals, star icon on point-tiles); 1x Trump Dial (PLA, 10cm disc with 6 engraved rune symbols around the rim and a rotating center pointer arm on a peg joint); 4x tile racks (PLA, 20cm slotted holders to keep a hand of tiles upright and hidden, one per player); 2x partnership score tracks (PLA, 15cm linear tracks 0-150 with pegs); box (printed-lid rigid box, 24x16x6cm).
ideas.demand_case: Trick-taking is a long-established core BGG mechanic category with sustained hobbyist demand (Skat, Euchre, Texas 42, and modern hits like The Crew all rank highly), and domino-based trick-taking specifically has a documented multi-generational fanbase in Texas 42 (an officially recognized state game of Texas with organized tournaments), evidencing real demand for tile-based (not card-based) trick-taking mechanics. Target audience: card/trick-taking game hobbyists and traditional domino-game players, ages 12+, who enjoy partnership trick-taking and want a physical tile alternative to a standard card deck.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a double bluff: which suit do I reveal by my orientation choice, and do I spend a strong rune now while I don't control trump, or hold it for a trick after my partner wins and sets a trump I can exploit — this adds a genuine hidden-information layer (opponents can't be certain which suit you'll show until the tile lands) on top of the suit-following tension that makes Texas 42 and Euchre-style trick-taking replayable for decades, while the dynamic trick-by-trick trump keeps every trick's stakes fresh rather than settling into one fixed trump suit for the whole hand.
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 distinct part types, ~90 total pieces including 4 identical tile racks. No paper cards anywhere — tiles are engraved dominoes, a well-established printable card substitute already common in tile-based games. The Trump Dial's rotating pointer-on-peg is a simple, low-risk single-joint mechanism (same class as a game spinner), needing only a stated 0.3mm clearance, not physical iteration. Tile racks are a simple slotted channel, no moving parts. No feature under 1mm (engraved rune symbols are 4mm, value numerals 3mm). No hardware/inserts required.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a mystical rune-themed trick-taking board game: a spread of rectangular domino-style tiles on a dark slate table, each engraved with two different glowing-carved rune symbols per tile in teal ink, arranged in a fan. Four wooden-look tile racks holding upright rows of tiles. In the center, a round rotating dial with six rune symbols around its rim and a bronze pointer arm resting on one symbol. A rectangular box beside it with lid art of interlocking runes in a circular pattern, titled 'RUNE TRICK' in angular carved-stone lettering. Moody atmospheric lighting, slate-grey/teal/bronze color palette, crisp matte 3D-printed tiles with engraved detail.

ideas.title: Guild Hollow
ideas.concept: A worker-placement game where your gear-shaped worker tokens earn a bonus for both players whenever they land next to a rival's gear, turning the usual 'block your opponent' tension into a 'who do I want to work next to' calculation. A turn feels like: scan the board for the slot that gets you the best resource AND lands you next to a rival gear for the shared payout, then commit a worker.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: standard worker placement (Agricola/Caylus-style single-worker-per-slot blocking). Genuine rule change: placement slots are arranged so certain pairs of adjacent slots are 'meshed' (marked with a printed gear-tooth connector line); if a player places a worker into a meshed slot that already has ANY other player's worker in its paired slot, BOTH players immediately gain a small bonus resource — replacing pure denial-based blocking with an added cooperative-adjacency incentive layer, so players must weigh grabbing a slot to deny opponents against grabbing a slot to trigger a shared bonus with them. Searched 'worker placement board game gear shaped meshing pieces adjacency bonus mechanic' and 'worker placement adjacent slot bonus both players shared resource mechanic' — found only generic worker-placement mechanic overviews and unrelated 'spatial worker placement' prototypes with no adjacency-bonus rule; no shipped worker-placement game was found where placing next to a rival's worker grants both players a bonus rather than simply blocking a slot.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 12+, 60-75 min, 5 rounds. SETUP: assemble the hex Guild Board with 12 Building slots; 4 pairs of adjacent slots are marked with a printed gear-tooth connector line ('meshed pairs'). Each player takes 2 gear-shaped worker tokens, a starting stock of 3 wood, 3 stone, 2 coin tokens, and a personal Guildhall mat. TURN ORDER: in player order, each player places ONE worker per turn (not both at once), alternating until all workers are placed for the round. PLACEMENT: place a worker on any empty Building slot; immediately gain that building's printed resource yield. If the slot you just placed into is part of a meshed pair AND the paired slot already holds an opposing player's worker, both you and that opponent immediately gain 1 extra coin token each (the 'mesh bonus'), regardless of whose turn it is. A slot may hold at most 2 workers total (from any combination of players); a 2nd worker placed into an already-occupied (non-meshed-triggering) slot yields only half the printed resource (round down), representing crowding. BUILD PHASE: after all workers are placed each round, any player may spend resources to purchase Structure tokens (printed small building pieces, costs vary 2-4 resources) worth printed VP, placing them on their Guildhall mat. CLEANUP: all workers return to their owners; round marker advances. GAME END: after 5 rounds, sum VP from all built Structures plus 1 VP per 3 leftover resources. Highest total wins.
ideas.components: 1x hex Guild Board (PLA, 30cm across, 12 engraved building slots with printed resource icons, 4 gear-tooth connector lines marking meshed pairs); 8x gear-shaped worker tokens (PLA, 2cm flat gear discs, 2 per player x4 colors); 4x Guildhall player mats (PLA, 15x15cm flat reference boards with structure-slot outlines); ~40x resource tokens (PLA, 1.2cm tokens in 3 shapes/colors for wood/stone/coin); ~24x Structure tokens (PLA, small 2cm building-silhouette pieces in 4 building types, VP value engraved on base); 1x Round tracker (PLA, 10cm track with peg); box (printed-lid rigid box, 28x28x7cm).
ideas.demand_case: Worker placement is one of BGG's largest and most consistently popular heavy-mechanic categories (Agricola, Caylus, Lords of Waterdeep all rank among the site's top-rated games), evidencing a large, durable hobbyist audience for this exact turn structure. Target audience: mid-to-heavy-weight hobbyist gamers, ages 12+, who enjoy classic worker-placement Euros and want a fresh tension beyond pure slot-blocking.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a genuinely new calculation layered onto a proven engine: do I take the objectively best resource slot, or do I take a slightly worse slot specifically because it's meshed with a rival's worker and grants us both a bonus, effectively trading a competitive edge for guaranteed extra value — a real strategic wrinkle absent from pure-blocking worker placement (Agricola, Caylus) that comparable placement-with-interaction games (Lords of Waterdeep's shared quest-completion bonuses) show can add table interaction and reduce runaway-blocking frustration without slowing the core loop down.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 distinct part types, ~85 total pieces. No cards; all buildings/resources are engraved boards and shaped tokens. Gear-shaped workers are purely decorative silhouettes (flat discs with gear-tooth edge detailing) — they do NOT physically mesh or interlock with each other, avoiding any need for precision tooth-engagement tolerances; adjacency is determined by board position only, which sidesteps the compounding-joint risk that real interlocking gears would introduce. No feature under 1mm (gear-tooth edge relief is 2mm, resource icons 3mm). No hardware or hinges required anywhere.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a medieval guild-themed worker placement board game: a hexagonal wooden-look board with twelve engraved building icons (forge, mill, tavern, market, etc.) connected by a few gold gear-tooth connector lines linking pairs of slots. Small flat gear-shaped worker tokens in red, blue, green, and yellow sit on various slots. Beside the board, four square guildhall player mats with small building-silhouette tokens and colorful resource tokens (brown wood cubes, grey stone cubes, gold coin discs). A square box with lid art of an ornate cog-and-guild-crest emblem, titled 'GUILD HOLLOW' in medieval serif lettering. Warm tavern-like lighting, amber/forest-green/stone-grey palette, crisp matte 3D-printed plastic pieces.

ideas.title: Teetering Peaks
ideas.concept: Four separate mini mountains grow from a shared base plate as players draft and stack numbered wedge pieces, and each round everyone secretly bets a flag peg on which peak they think will still be standing tallest. A turn feels like: pick a wedge, decide which peak to risk it on, and watch the table hold its breath as pieces balance higher and higher.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: single-tower balance/dexterity stacking games (Tetra Tower, Cheese Wedge-style stacking, where the whole game is decided by one tower's collapse and elimination). Genuine rule change: instead of one shared tower, the board has 4 independently-stacked peaks, and each round players place a colored Flag-Peg claim on top of whichever peak they predict will survive AND be tallest at that round's reveal — adding a prediction/betting layer on top of the physical stacking skill, and toppled peaks are removed from THAT round's scoring only (the game continues with the remaining peaks) rather than ending the whole game on a single collapse. Searched 'dexterity board game stacking wedge tiles king of the hill tabletop' and 'dexterity balance stacking game wedge shaped pieces build tower without toppling player elimination' — found Tetra Tower and Cheese Wedge Stacking Game (both single-tower, tallest-tower-wins or last-to-topple-loses formats with no multi-zone board or prediction-betting layer) and an unrelated card-based 'King of the Hill' game (no dexterity/stacking component); no shipped dexterity game was found combining multiple simultaneous stacking zones with a round-based prediction-claim scoring layer.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 8+, 25-30 min, 3 rounds. SETUP: place the square Base Plate in the table center; it has 4 marked Peak Zones (one in each corner). Shuffle the 40 numbered wedge pieces (values 1-5, each a truncated-prism balance shape like Tetra Tower's pieces) into a bag. ROUND STRUCTURE: each round has a Build Phase and a Claim Phase. BUILD PHASE: players take turns drawing one wedge blind from the bag and must place it onto any ONE of the 4 Peaks (their choice), following the physical rule that it must balance without any part of the wedge below it moving or the peak visibly toppling — if it topples, that whole Peak's current stack is removed from the base plate and set aside (out of the game for scoring this round; that Peak zone restarts empty for the next round), and the toppling player also returns 1 wedge of their choice from their scored pile (if any) back to the bag as a small penalty. Continue drafting/placing until every player has placed 3 wedges this round. CLAIM PHASE: simultaneously, all players secretly choose one Flag-Peg and, on a 3-2-1 count, plant it on top of whichever Peak (of those still standing) they predict is currently the tallest; reveal all flags together. SCORING: the tallest surviving Peak (measured by printed height ruler on the Base Plate) scores 3 points to each player whose flag is on it, the second-tallest scores 1 point to each player whose flag is on it; no points for flags on shorter or toppled peaks. GAME END: after 3 rounds, sum each player's claim points; highest total wins; ties broken by total number of wedges that player successfully placed without toppling across the game.
ideas.components: 1x square Base Plate (PLA, 25x25cm flat plate with 4 raised marked Peak Zones ~6cm diameter each and a printed height-measuring ruler along one edge); 40x numbered wedge pieces (PLA, truncated-prism shapes ~4-6cm long, values 1-5 engraved on the flat face, designed with a flat stable base and gently tapered stacking faces per proven balance-stacking geometry); 4x sets of Flag-Peg claim markers (PLA, 6cm flag-topped pegs, 4 colors, 3 per player for 3 rounds); box (printed-lid rigid box, 27x27x8cm, doubles as wedge storage tray with printed dividers).
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity/stacking games are a well-established BGG mechanic category with proven mass-market success (Jenga remains one of the best-selling games of all time, and modern balance-stacking entries like Tetra Tower have sustained retail presence), evidencing strong demand for tactile physical-skill games at family gatherings. Target audience: family and party-game buyers, ages 8+, who enjoy Jenga/Tetra Tower-style tactile stacking but want more table interaction than a single winner-take-all elimination.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn has two layers: a physical-skill placement choice (which peak can I safely add height to without toppling it) and a social-prediction choice (which peak do I bet will end up tallest, potentially betting on a rival's peak I intentionally didn't help build) — this combines the visceral tension that makes Jenga-style stacking so immediately engaging with a light bluffing/prediction layer that keeps eliminated players in the game (unlike single-tower dexterity games where one collapse can end your participation), which comparable multi-round push-your-luck-plus-dexterity hybrids show extends replay value for a 25-30 minute family slot.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 distinct part types, ~65 total pieces. No cards. The wedge-stacking geometry follows the same truncated-prism balance profile as existing shipped dexterity stacking products (Tetra Tower, Cheese Wedge Stacking), which is documented, proven-printable geometry — not a novel unvalidated mechanism — so fairness/balance behavior can be reasoned about from the established flat-base tapered-face design rather than requiring open-ended physical iteration; only the base flatness (must be printed with a raft or brim to guarantee a true-flat stacking surface) needs a stated tolerance note. Flag-pegs are simple friction-fit peg-in-recess, low risk. No feature under 1mm (engraved wedge numerals are 4mm). No hardware/inserts required.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a colorful family dexterity board game: a square flat base plate on a table with four small mountain-peak stacks of angular numbered wooden-look wedge pieces rising from each corner in warm amber and cream tones, one peak taller than the rest, small flag-topped pegs in red, blue, green, and yellow planted on top of two of the peaks. A square box beside it with lid art of four jagged mountain silhouettes with tiny flags at their summits, titled 'TEETERING PEAKS' in bold playful lettering. Bright cheerful lighting, amber/cream/multicolor flag palette, crisp matte 3D-printed wedge pieces with visible engraved numerals.

ideas.title: Sundial Market
ideas.concept: Players bid for goods by pushing a personal peg further along a shared inward spiral track, but pegs never reset between rounds, so every aggressive early bid permanently eats into the limited distance you have left for the rest of the game. A turn feels like: watching how far a rival is willing to push their peg toward the market's center, deciding whether this good is worth spending irreplaceable future bidding room on.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'board game auction bidding spiral track physical peg escalating bid mechanism' and 'auction board game shared scarce track bid never resets across rounds mechanic' — found only generic auction-mechanic overviews (Bombard Games, BGG mechanic pages), a peg-based betting patent ('Game of Donuts'), and standard chip/money-based auction games (High-Bid, QE) where currency is separately tracked and typically resettable or replenished each round. No shipped board game was found using a single physical spiral distance track as BOTH the bid amount AND a permanently-spent global resource carried across all auction rounds of the game.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players, ages 12+, 45 min, 8 rounds. SETUP: place the Spiral Bid Track board in the center (a flat spiral groove with 30 numbered steps winding inward from the rim to the central Market Hub). Each player takes a Bid Peg and places it at step 0 (the outer rim start point, off the numbered spiral proper). Shuffle the 24 Goods Tiles (each engraved with a good icon and a printed Value 1-8) into a bag; reveal 1 at the start of each round (8 rounds total, 8 tiles used, 16 held in reserve for game-to-game variety across multiple plays). ROUND: (1) Reveal the round's Goods Tile in the Market Hub. (2) Starting with the player currently furthest back on the spiral (least distance spent) and going in ascending distance order, each player in turn either PASSES (steps out of bidding for this round, taking no action) or BIDS by moving their Bid Peg forward along the spiral to any step further than the current highest bid this round (minimum 1 step further); a player who passes cannot re-enter that round's bidding. Continue until only one active bidder remains among those who haven't passed. (3) That player wins the Goods Tile (place it on their personal Storefront mat) — their peg stays exactly where it stopped; it does NOT return to 0. GAME END: after 8 rounds (or immediately if any player's peg reaches step 30, the Market Hub, at which point that player must pass on all remaining rounds — they're 'bid out'). SCORING: sum the printed Value of all Goods Tiles on your Storefront, plus a banked-efficiency bonus equal to (30 minus your final peg position) divided by 3, rounded down. Highest total wins.
ideas.components: 1x Spiral Bid Track board (PLA, 30cm diameter flat spiral groove board, 30 numbered steps winding to a central raised Market Hub platform); 5x Bid Pegs (PLA, 4cm colored pegs sized to sit in the spiral groove, 5 colors); 24x Goods Tiles (PLA, 3cm hex chips, engraved good icon + printed value numeral 1-8); 5x Storefront player mats (PLA, 15x10cm flat mats with tile-holding recesses); box (printed-lid rigid box, 32x32x6cm).
ideas.demand_case: Auction/bidding is a well-established BGG mechanic category with a long track record of hobbyist and family success (Ra, For Sale, Modern Art, High Society all rank as enduring genre staples), evidencing durable demand for competitive bidding gameplay across different weight classes. Target audience: mid-weight hobbyist gamers, ages 12+, who enjoy classic auction games (Ra, For Sale) and want a fresh physical spin on how bids are tracked and constrained.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a genuinely scarce-resource tension unusual for the auction genre: because your bid position never resets, every early aggressive bid is not just spending money you'll earn back next round (as in most auction games) but permanently narrowing your total future bidding ceiling for the rest of the game — forcing a long-horizon budgeting problem layered on top of the classic 'how much is this worth to me right now' auction read that makes Ra and For Sale replayable, which should sharpen end-game tension since players can visibly see exactly how much runway their rivals have left on the shared spiral.
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 distinct part types, ~54 total pieces. No cards; goods are engraved hex chips. The Spiral Bid Track is a single static engraved groove board with pegs sitting in it — no moving/rotating assembly at all, making this one of the lowest-risk producibility profiles in the batch (comparable to a simple cribbage-style peg track, a long-proven printable joint type). No feature under 1mm (spiral groove width 5mm, step numerals 3mm engraved). No hardware or hinges required anywhere.

Beside the board, small hexagonal chips engraved with market-goods icons (spice jar, cloth bolt, gem, urn) and numeral values, arranged on rectangular storefront mats. A square box with lid art of a stylized sundial-market emblem with radiating market stalls, titled 'SUNDIAL MARKET' in elegant serif lettering.
